summary: In a single recent year, fires burned an area larger than India. Two decades of NASA satellite records could show where fire activity is about to become unusual, but MODIS and VIIRS see the same fires differently, so their records cannot be compared directly. MODVIIRS solves this. We harmonized 185.7 million MODIS and VIIRS detections across Mexico, Brazil, Russia, Australia, Angola and DR Congo (persistent heat sources removed, unified confidence, per-sensor-era normalization), cutting the false anomalies caused by the sensor switch by up to half. On that consistent record, a machine-learning model fed with NASA POWER weather estimates, every week and for every zone, the probability that hotspot activity will exceed its own historical 90th percentile. Tested on data it never saw, it ranks risky zones far better than historical averages (live 2026 season, Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico: AUC 0.86 vs 0.61 and 4.6x the average precision). An interactive 3D web map lets anyone select a region, explore its harmonized history and read the forecast as a clear alert level. A hotspot is not a wildfire: MODVIIRS is an early-warning layer that helps fire agencies decide where to look first.
details:
MODVIIRS – HARMONIZED MODIS + VIIRS FIRE RECORDS AND WEEKLY EARLY WARNING

Two Satellites, One Fire, Two Different Stories

NASA has watched every fire on Earth from orbit for more than two decades, first with MODIS (1 km) and now with VIIRS (375 m). But the two sensors do not see the same planet: VIIRS detects many more small fires, sees them at different times of day and has changed platforms (S-NPP, then NOAA-20). Mix their records naively and recent years look "abnormal" simply because the instrument changed. That is the gap MODVIIRS closes: first make the record honest, then use it to look ahead.

What exactly does it do?

For any region the user selects on a 3D globe, MODVIIRS answers two questions:

What has fire activity really looked like?

A harmonized MODIS + VIIRS history: daily hotspot and fire radiative power (FRP) series, a monthly anomaly calendar, typical seasonality, intensity classes and per-step statistics, all comparable across sensors and years.

What is coming?

A weekly early-warning forecast: "the system anticipates with X% probability anomalous hotspot activity in week T in zone Z", shown as a reliability score and calendar for the selected dates, how the forecast compared with what actually happened in past years, its error against a historical-average baseline and its accuracy year by year.

HISTORY tab: harmonized VIIRS record of the Yucatán Peninsula, 2012–2025 — 880,451 hotspots, daily series and intensity calendar.

How does it work?

1. Harmonization (the heart of the challenge).

Keep nominal- and high-confidence detections, mapped to a common confidence scale. Remove persistent heat sources (industry, gas flares, volcanoes) with a 0.01° mask built from 60+ months of detections. Measure activity as "fire-days" per 0.1° cell, a metric much less sensitive to pixel size than raw counts. Normalize every statistic within its sensor era (Aqua MODIS; S-NPP VIIRS; S-NPP + NOAA-20 VIIRS), so each period is compared with its own baseline.

2. Anomaly definition.

A zone-week is anomalous when its fire-days exceed max(p90, 3), where p90 comes from the same zone, the same time of year (±2 weeks), previous years only and the same sensor era. No future information is ever used.

3. Forecast model.

A gradient-boosting classifier (scikit-learn HistGradientBoosting) learns from recent activity (1–4 weeks back, relative to each zone's own threshold), seasonality, the zone's historical anomaly frequency, a regional signal and NASA POWER weather (30- and 90-day rainfall and its anomaly, consecutive dry days, humidity, maximum temperature, wind).

4. Two scales.

Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico: 0.5° zones (~55 km), running live in 2026 with FIRMS near-real-time data. Six countries (Mexico, Brazil, Russia, Australia, Angola, DR Congo): 1° zones (~110 km), 4,492 zones.

5. Web platform.

A Flask API documented with Swagger serves harmonized data and forecasts; a React + TypeScript + MapLibre interface provides the globe, the timeline, and an analysis panel with HISTORY and PREDICTIONS tabs.

PREDICTIONS tab: how reliable the weekly forecast is for the selected dates (76%, very reliable) and a reliability calendar, Yucatán Peninsula.

Harmonization in Numbers

Year | False anomalies, sensors mixed | False anomalies, harmonized
2015 | 16.4% | 8.8%
2019 | 16.7% | 10.4%

Share of zone-weeks flagged as anomalous, Yucatán Peninsula: mixing MODIS and VIIRS (red) vs. normalizing per sensor era (blue).

The Decisive Difference: Tested Live in 2026

Every number below is out of sample. In walk-forward validation, each year is predicted by a model trained only on earlier years.

Test | MODVIIRS | Historical-average baseline
Yucatán, VIIRS era 2015–2025 (AUC) | 0.853 | 0.588
Yucatán, live 2026 season, 44 weeks (AUC) | 0.860 | 0.608
Yucatán, live 2026 (average precision) | 0.325 | 0.071 (4.6x)
Six countries 2023–2025 (AUC) | 0.73–0.94 | 0.53–0.61

By country: Russia 0.94, Mexico 0.85, Australia 0.85, Angola 0.84, Brazil 0.83, DR Congo 0.73.

NASA POWER weather improves accuracy in 18 of 18 country-years (Wilcoxon p = 0.0002).

Real case: in the week of May 18, 2026, the forecast for the Yucatán Peninsula reached 62% (Critical), and 11 zones broke their seasonal record.

Against CONAFOR official fire records (Mexico), the forecast captures WHEN fire seasons intensify; exact location agreement at this scale is still limited.

Inside the PREDICTIONS tab: forecast vs. what happened in past years, forecast error vs. a historical-average baseline (25% lower), accuracy by year and calibration.

What benefits does it have?

For scientists: a consistent 20+ year MODIS + VIIRS record without artificial trends caused by the sensor change.

For fire agencies and civil protection: a weekly early-warning layer to prioritize surveillance, brigades and prevention where activity is about to become unusual.

For everyone: explainable alerts. Each one traces back to the zone's own history, its threshold and the weather, and is presented in plain language.

What do we hope to achieve?

In the short term, run the six-country model live every week with FIRMS near-real-time data, as the Yucatán Peninsula already does, and share it with fire management agencies such as Mexico's CONAFOR.

In the long term, extend the harmonized record and the forecast to every fire-prone country, add longer forecast horizons, and validate locally with national agencies, including Space Apps partner agencies in countries we already cover, such as Angola and Brazil.

Factors we considered

Honesty of the signal: a hotspot is not a wildfire, so we forecast anomalous hotspot activity, not fires.

No data leakage: thresholds and features only use information available before the forecast week.

Sensor eras: a single platform per era for the forecast, so a new satellite never looks like a fire surge.

Limitations stated openly: probabilities above 50% are somewhat optimistic; the six-country model currently replays 2023–2025, while the Yucatán Peninsula runs live.

Tools, languages and software

Data processing & ML: Python, pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, Polars, scikit-learn, SciPy

Backend & API: Flask, Flasgger (Swagger/OpenAPI)

Frontend & UI: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL

DevOps: Git, GitHub, GitHub Actions (CI)

Data sources: NASA FIRMS, NASA POWER, NASA GIBS, CONAFOR
